allopack.standards: NGSS 3-5-ETS1-1 (define a simple design problem reflecting a need, with criteria and constraints); NGSS 3-5-ETS1-2 (generate and compare multiple possible solutions to a problem); CCSS.ELA-LITERACY.RI.5.7 (draw on information from multiple sources to answer a question). NOTE: NGSS has no dedicated simple-machines performance expectation — this pack supports engineering-design work and classic force/motion instruction rather than claiming an alignment it does not earn.

data.body:
**Due:** (your teacher will tell you)

A machine cannot give you something for nothing. Every one of them makes the same trade, and once you see it you cannot unsee it.

1. Read **The Deal** — the last paragraph is the point of the whole lesson.
2. Learn the six machines in the **Glossary**, then win the **Matching** game.
3. Keep the **Six Machines** chart open while you look around the room.
4. Sort the objects in **Which Machine Is It?** — two of them are arguments.
5. Take the quiz. Question 4 asks about the trade, which is the real idea.
6. Use the **Sentence Frames** to explain a machine you actually use.
7. Lock the ideas in with **Remember the Six Machines** — study the example aid, then make one your own.
8. Finish with **Design Challenge: Lift the Water Jug** — use what you learned on a real problem, and mark every guess as a guess.

Challenge while you work: find five simple machines in the room you are sitting in right now. There are more than you think. ⚙️

history.title: The Deal
history.data:
## The Deal

A machine does not make you stronger. It changes how your strength gets used — and it always charges you for the favor.

There are six classic **simple machines**, and everything mechanical you have ever touched is built from them.

A **lever** is a stiff bar that turns on a fixed point called a **fulcrum**. Push down on one end and the other end lifts. A crowbar, a seesaw, a bottle opener, and the bones in your arm are all levers.

An **inclined plane** is a ramp. Walking a heavy box up a ramp takes less force than lifting it straight up — but you have to travel farther to get it to the same height.

A **wedge** is really an inclined plane that moves. An axe, a knife, a nail, and your front teeth all drive a thin edge into something and push it apart.

A **screw** is an inclined plane wrapped around a post. Look closely at the threads — that spiral is a ramp that has been rolled up. Turning the screw many times pulls it forward a small distance with great force.

A **wheel and axle** is a wheel fixed to a rod so they turn together. Doorknobs, steering wheels, and screwdrivers all use it. A small turn at the wide outer edge produces a strong twist at the narrow center.

A **pulley** is a wheel with a groove for a rope. One pulley changes the direction you pull — handy, because pulling down is easier than lifting up. Add more pulleys and you also reduce the force needed, though you must pull more rope.

Now the deal, which is the same in every case: **you trade distance for force.** Use half the force, move twice as far. Use a quarter of the force, move four times as far. A machine never reduces the total work — it just spreads it out into a form your body can manage.

And every real machine charges a small extra fee called **friction**, which turns a bit of your effort into heat. That is why rubbing your hands warms them and why machines need grease.

So when someone says a machine makes work easier, they mean something precise. Not less work. Less force at any one moment, paid for with more distance — a trade that is almost always worth making.

data.def: A stiff bar that turns on a fixed point to lift or move something.
The fixed point a lever turns on.
A grooved wheel with a rope, used to change the direction or size of a pull.
A moving inclined plane with a thin edge that splits things apart.
An inclined plane wrapped around a post, turning rotation into strong forward force.
A ramp — a flat surface set at an angle to reduce lifting force.
The rod a wheel is fixed to, turning together with it.
What happens when a force moves something a distance.
The rubbing force that resists motion and turns some effort into heat.
The force YOU apply to a machine.
The thing the machine is moving or lifting for you.

data.title: Remember the Six Machines
data.instructions: Each card locks in facts from The Deal. Study the example aid, make it yours, and explain how it leads back to the trade every machine makes.
data.sourceExcerpt: There are six classic simple machines: lever, inclined plane, wedge, screw, wheel and axle, pulley. You trade distance for force. Use half the force, move twice as far. A machine never reduces the total work. Every real machine charges a small extra fee called friction.

essentialFacts: Lever: a stiff bar turning on a fulcrum.
Inclined plane: a ramp; a wedge is a ramp that moves; a screw is a ramp wrapped around a post.
Wheel and axle: a wheel fixed to a rod so they turn together.
Pulley: a grooved wheel with a rope that changes the direction or size of a pull.
cards.aiExample: L.I.W.S.W.P. — Lazy Inventors Want Simple Work, Please: Lever, Inclined plane, Wedge, Screw, Wheel and axle, Pulley.
cards.mapping: Six words, six machines, and the sentence itself says what machines are for: making work feel simpler. The three middle letters (I, W, S) are the ramp family, which helps you remember they are related.
scaffoldSteps: Write the six machines and circle the first letters.
Build a sentence; try to make the I-W-S words go together since those machines are all ramps.
Read it back and point to a real object for each letter.
coachPrompts: Can you group the three ramp machines inside your sentence?
cards.studentPrompt: Write your own six-word sentence or reorder the example.
cards.reasoningPrompt: Explain how each word points to a machine and what that machine does.

hookFact.text: The bones in your arm are levers, and your front teeth are wedges.

cards.target: The deal: less force, more distance, same work (plus a friction fee)
essentialFacts: A machine trades distance for force: half the force means moving twice as far.
A machine never reduces the total work; it spreads the work into a form your body can manage.
Friction turns a little of your effort into heat, so real machines always cost slightly more than the trade alone.
cards.aiExample: Paying for a bike in installments: the price never changes, you just pay smaller amounts more times. A machine lets you pay for work in smaller pushes over a longer distance, and friction is the small fee on every payment.
cards.mapping: Total price maps to total work, each installment maps to the smaller force, the number of payments maps to the longer distance, and the fee maps to friction.
cards.scaffoldStarter: A machine is like paying for ____ in ____: the total stays ____, but each ____ is smaller.
scaffoldSteps: Choose something you pay for a little at a time.
Match total, installment, and number of payments to work, force, and distance.
Add where friction shows up as an extra cost.
coachPrompts: What in your analogy shows that the total never goes down?
cards.studentPrompt: Write your own analogy for the distance-for-force trade.
cards.reasoningPrompt: How does your analogy show why a machine cannot give you something for nothing?

hookFact.text: A machine does not make you stronger. It changes how your strength gets used, and it always charges you for the favor.

cards.target: Machines in disguise: wedge and screw are inclined planes
essentialFacts: A wedge is an inclined plane that moves: an axe, a knife, a nail, your front teeth.
A screw is an inclined plane wrapped around a post; the threads are a rolled-up ramp.
Turning a screw many times pulls it forward a small distance with great force.
cards.aiExample: WEDGE = a ramp on the MOVE (it drives into things). SCREW = a ramp that SPIRALS (unroll the threads and you get a ramp).
cards.mapping: Both keywords keep the word ramp attached to the machine, so when you see a knife or a jar lid you see the inclined plane hiding inside it.
cards.scaffoldStarter: A wedge is a ramp that ____. A screw is a ramp that ____.
scaffoldSteps: Say what a ramp does: makes a climb gentler over a longer path.
Describe what happens when the ramp moves (wedge) and when it wraps (screw).
Find one real object for each.
coachPrompts: If you unrolled a screw's thread, how long would the ramp be compared to the screw?
cards.studentPrompt: Write your own two keyword links.
cards.reasoningPrompt: How do your keywords prove a knife and a bolt are the same machine underneath?

history.title: Machine Check

questions.question: What is the fulcrum of a lever?
options: The heavy object being lifted
The fixed point the bar turns on
The force you apply
The long end of the bar
questions.correctAnswer: The fixed point the bar turns on

questions.question: A screw is really which simple machine in disguise?
options: A lever bent into a circle
Two pulleys joined together
An inclined plane wrapped around a post
A wedge with a wheel attached
questions.correctAnswer: An inclined plane wrapped around a post

questions.question: Why is pushing a heavy box up a ramp easier than lifting it straight up?
options: The box actually weighs less once it is on a ramp
Ramps work by removing friction from the surface entirely
Gravity stops pulling on objects that sit on a ramp
You use less force, but you travel a longer distance
questions.correctAnswer: You use less force, but you travel a longer distance

questions.question: A machine lets you lift a load using half the force. What does it cost you?
options: You must move roughly twice the distance
Nothing at all, because machines add strength for free
The load you are lifting becomes twice as heavy
You must move the load twice as quickly to make up for it
questions.correctAnswer: You must move roughly twice the distance

questions.question: What does friction do in every real machine?
options: Adds extra energy that increases the machine's total work
It only matters in machines that use wheels or axles
Turns some of your effort into heat, so a little is always lost
Builds up until it makes the machine stop working entirely
questions.correctAnswer: Turns some of your effort into heat, so a little is always lost

questions.question: Explain why a single pulley at the top of a flagpole is useful even though it does not reduce the force needed.
questions.expectedAnswer: It changes the DIRECTION of the pull. Instead of climbing the pole and lifting the flag upward, you can stand on the ground and pull down, which is much easier for a person's body even though the force is the same.

questions.question: Your friend says 'machines let you do less work.' Correct the statement precisely.
questions.expectedAnswer: Machines do not reduce the total work. They reduce the FORCE needed at any moment by making you move a longer distance, and friction actually makes the total effort slightly greater. The work is spread out, not removed.

reflections.text: Which simple machine do you use most in a normal day without thinking about it?
Design a machine to move something heavy in your home. Which type would you use and why?

history.title: Machine Questions

data.question: Could ancient people really move those enormous stones? 🗿
data.answer: Yes, with ramps, levers, ropes, and enormous numbers of people. No lost technology is needed — simple machines plus organization explain the pyramids and Stonehenge, though archaeologists still debate the exact methods.

data.question: Is a bicycle a simple machine?
data.answer: It is a COMPOUND machine — several simple ones working together: wheels and axles, levers in the brakes and pedals, and screws holding it all in place.

data.question: Can a machine ever be 100% efficient? 🤔
data.answer: No real one. Friction always takes a cut, turning some effort into heat. Engineers reduce it with grease, bearings, and smooth surfaces, but nobody has ever eliminated it.

data.question: Why is a knife sharp instead of blunt?
data.answer: A thin edge concentrates your force onto a tiny area, which is what makes a wedge work. The same push on a blunt edge is spread out and just squashes things.

data.question: Are my body parts machines?
data.answer: Genuinely, yes. Your forearm is a lever with the elbow as fulcrum, your jaw is a lever, and your teeth are wedges. Biology is full of simple machines.

data.question: Why do screws grip so much better than nails? 🔩
data.answer: The thread is a long ramp wrapped around the shaft, so turning it many times converts a small twisting force into a very strong pull — plus those threads bite into the material and resist pulling out.

history.title: Design Challenge: Lift the Water Jug
history.meta: 5th-6th Grade • Design brief • a machine that lifts more than you can

data.title: Lift the Water Jug
data.instructions: Design a simple machine, or a combination of two, that lets one student lift a full five-gallon water jug onto a table using less force than lifting it by hand. Predict the trade you are making, then test it.
data.fitReason: The reading's claim that machines trade distance for force is easy to repeat and hard to feel. A design task with a real load makes students choose the trade and measure what it costs.

brief.context: The classroom water cooler sits on a table. Full replacement jugs weigh about 19 kilograms (over 40 pounds), too heavy for most students to lift safely onto the table. You have a sturdy plank, a wooden block, rope, two pulleys with hooks, a hand truck wheel, tape, and a spring scale that reads up to 10 kilograms of pull.
brief.audience: Your teacher and the students who refill the cooler
brief.drivingQuestion: Which simple machine, or pair of machines, lets one student raise the full jug onto the table with a pull the spring scale can measure, and exactly what does that machine cost us in distance?
brief.seedDirection: Start from the deal: if you want to pull with half the force, plan to move something twice as far. Which machine makes that trade in the space you have?
lockedLessonFacts: A lever is a stiff bar turning on a fulcrum; push down on one end and the other lifts.
An inclined plane lets you push a load up with less force over a longer path.
One pulley changes the direction of a pull; more pulleys reduce the force needed but you must pull more rope.
Every machine trades distance for force; the total work never decreases.
Friction turns some effort into heat, so a real machine costs a little more than the trade alone.
openQuestions: How long can the ramp be before it runs into the wall, and how steep does that make it?
Where should the fulcrum sit so the student's end goes down far enough?
How much rope do we need if two pulleys cut the force in half?
How much of our effort will friction eat on the plank?
stakeholders: Anyone standing nearby while a heavy jug moves
The teacher who must approve the setup
criteria: The jug reaches the table height safely with a measured pull of 10 kilograms or less
The team predicts the trade (how far the student moves for how much less force) before testing and compares it to the result
The design sheet names the machine and its parts with lesson vocabulary
Friction is measured or estimated and mentioned in the explanation
constraints: Nothing may be lifted more than waist high by hand
The jug must be secured so it cannot roll or fall
Setup and test fit in one class period
brief.deliverable: A labeled design drawing, a prediction (force before, force with machine, distance moved), a test table with spring-scale readings, and a short explanation of the trade using at least four glossary words.

parallelExample.context: Movers needed to get a piano into a truck bed a meter off the ground.
parallelExample.move: They laid a long ramp instead of lifting, then added a rope around a pulley on the truck so two people could pull from the truck bed. They accepted walking the piano four meters to gain one meter of height, and they waxed the ramp to cut friction.
parallelExample.whyItHelps: It is the same trade with the same two fixes you can use: a longer path for less force, and a pulley to change direction. Waxing the ramp is the friction fee being paid on purpose.

supports.frameStarter: We will use a ____ because it lets us ____. In exchange, we will have to ____.
frameChoices: A ramp from the floor to the table, pushing the jug up on the hand-truck wheel
A lever with the fulcrum near the jug so a small push lifts a heavy load
Two pulleys hooked above the table to halve the pull and change its direction
A ramp plus one pulley so the student pulls down instead of pushing up
coachPrompts: Where in your design does the extra distance show up: rope, ramp, or lever arm?
What would happen to your force reading if you made the ramp shorter?
How will you show that the total work did not get smaller?

data.coachHint: Measure the pull with the scale before you use the machine and after. The difference is the trade; the extra distance is the price.
data.sourceExcerpt: You trade distance for force. Use half the force, move twice as far. A machine never reduces the total work; it just spreads it out into a form your body can manage.
